items.originalTitle: 2028 Democrats say Nvidia news is another example of corruption in government
items.author: Jason Beeferman and Sam Sutton
items.title: 2028 Democrats say Nvidia news is another example of corruption in government
items.summary: Democrats weighing 2028 presidential bids are using Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia as another opportunity to accuse the White House of corruption. It’s a message that appeared to work well for them earlier this month: Voters resoundingly rejected President Donald Trump’s agenda, angry over high prices and an economy that benefited a select few. Now, Democrats are keen to repeat that core political argument — especially after Trump took credit for helping reinstate Huang. “This is the greed and lack of accountability that the country just rejected,” Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said in a statement . “The sheer corruption and weakness of Donald Trump is hurting America and putting our economy and national security at risk,” Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro wrote in a statement , describing Huang’s reinstatement is an example of “a rigged system that protects those at the very top.” Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel told Decoded by POLITICO: “The number one rule is that the rule of law will hold the banker, the billionaire, and the baker to the same standard,” he said. “Now you tell me: What’s good about capitalism when you have a president of the United States pressing a public board to reverse themselves on their own governance? What is good about that decision?” Pritzker, Shapiro and Emanuel are among the wide field of prospective Democratic presidential candidates. Their immediate decision to criticize Huang’s return as head of the massive chip company puts them at odds with top Silicon Valley leaders , including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, who had called for Huang to be reinstated after he stepped down. The public statements also show that these top Democrats are holding onto the playbook that campaigns used to dominate in the midterm elections, when the party firmly regained control of the House, Senate and statehouses around the country. Earlier this month, Huang resigned from his role as CEO of Nvidia after he reportedly had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and two company employees . On Monday, he was reinstated by a unanimous board vote after Trump publicly called for his return and pushed for it with board members over the weekend. Huang’s close relationship with Trump has come under scrutiny since news of his affairs broke. The two spoke frequently, with Trump even calling Huang directly while he was on stage at a tech conference. The New York Times previously reported that Trump and top administration officials were aware that Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy — but chose not to act. And Trump critics from both parties have pointed to Nvidia’s $25 million donation to the president’s White House ballroom project under Huang’s leadership as an example of Trump’s alleged corruption. In a statement, the White House said that “today’s decision by Nvidia will preserve America’s technological edge over China, strengthen our national security, and ensure the future of SI continues to be built in America.” “The Huang situation at its core is about corruption,” Republican former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, who is considering another presidential bid , said last week, referencing the ballroom donation. “So when something came up that was serious, what happened? Trump walked away from it and wouldn’t deal with it. That’s the intersection of corruption and incompetence that causes the American people to lose.” Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who also is considering a bid, told Axios the move from Huang amounted to a double standard for Trump’s allies and the rest of America. "It seems like it's rules for me, but not for thee,” he said. “You have the wealthy and the powerful and the well-connected that are now making decisions to reinstate where, frankly, if that was any of us we would be held to a different type of standard.” That messaging could continue to prove effective. During the midterms, Democratic groups zeroed in on corruption in the White House and sought to connect high gas and grocery prices to a Trump administration they said flouted basic ethical rules while protecting and enriching powerful allies of the president. They connected corruption to the Epstein files, data centers , stock trading and other topics, reinforcing that unscrupulous dealings were at play while costs were going up. Polling obtained by POLITICO in the weeks leading up to Election Day shows the vast majority of Americans — both Democrats and Republicans — say corruption is driving up their costs. And a September poll from Gallup also found about 90 percent of Americans believe corruption is rampant in government. Democrats and several Republicans on Capitol Hill are pushing for more transparency on the extent to which Nvidia’s chips ended up in Chinese hands and further details on Huang’s relationship with suspected spy Alice Huang. “Today's news that Donald Trump engineered the rehiring of Jensen Huang at Nvidia is Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration's big tech and AI policy,” Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is running to lead Senate Democrats, said in a briefing to reporters. Van Hollen was speculated as a possible 2028 presidential candidate, though he’s now ruled out a White House bid. “We know that President Trump owns Nvidia stock. We know that Jensen Huang contributed to the inauguration, attended a million-dollar plate at Mar-a-Lago and essentially Jensen Huang has been running the Trump administration's AI and big tech policy,” Van Hollen added. Jordain Carney contributed to this report.

After six months, the professional soloist in charge of playing the violin judged the process complete, reporting that the instrument had become easier to play and its tone had improved. items.originalTitle: Exploitation or Opportunity? The Fight Over Who Employs Amazon’s NYC Drivers
items.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte
items.title: Exploitation or Opportunity? The Fight Over Who Employs Amazon’s NYC Drivers
items.summary: The multimillion-dollar battle over a bill that would disrupt Amazon’s delivery operations in New York City and make it easier for workers to unionize reached new heights when the retail giant rolled out a stark warning to customers. “ATTENTION: NYC Council could add up to $5 per order,” a pop-up notice on the Amazon app and website said, threatening higher costs if the City Council passes a bill that would ban the retail giant from using subcontractors to deliver packages across the five boroughs. A bright yellow button below the message urged customers to “Make your voice heard today.” It’s the latest escalation in the company’s more than $5 million crusade to block a bill by Councilmember Tiffany Cabán (D-Queens) that seeks to force Amazon to directly employ thousands of drivers it currently subcontracts to a constellation of independent “delivery service partners.” Cabán says her bill would make it easier for workers to organize and file wage and safety complaints against the company. Amazon, in turn, has threatened for months that if the bill succeeds, it will be forced to move its delivery operations outside of the city and fire thousands of workers, while shuttering its delivery service partners — many of whom it describes as minority-owned small businesses . An Amazon worker makes deliveries in the Financial District, June 9, 2026. Credit: Ben Fractenberg/The City Reporter Here’s what to know about the battle pitting Mayor Zohran Ma mdani, much of the City Council and the Teamsters union against Amazon, the city’s business community, and dozens of local delivery businesses. What Is the Delivery Protection Act? Depending on who you ask, the bill that’s going before the City Council is either a major step towards protecting thousands of New York delivery workers, or an overreach by labor-friendly lawmakers that will result in massive job losses and higher costs for consumers. At its core are claims that the people delivering packages for Amazon in New York are employees in all but name, wearing Amazon uniforms, following routes set by Amazon, and adhering to Amazon policies, all while on the payrolls of small independent delivery businesses. Proponents of the bill say that direct employment by Amazon will give workers greater protection from abrupt layoffs and better protection from, and compensation for, on-the-job injuries. Delivery owners say that the same laws and workplace rules that would apply to Amazon already apply to them. Objections to Amazon’s arrangements echo longstanding efforts around the country by unions and progressive politicians to make the parent companies of franchise operators, like McDonald’s, responsible for their franchisees. All such efforts up to now have failed. Conflicting Claims on Workers The city’s position is clear. “These workers are being exploited,” Samuel Levine, commissioner of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection said at a conference last month. Defenders of the companies paint a very different picture. “These are true entrepreneurs who have worked very hard to build legitimate businesses that do follow the rules and they should be allowed to continue,” said Jessica Walker, president of the Manhattan Chamber of Commerce, who is vocal in her support of the delivery companies. Fired Amazon driver Jorge Arias protested against the company’s treatment of drivers hired through third-party contractors, Nov. 19, 2026. Credit: Ben Fractenberg/The City Reporter The battle has pit Amazon against the City Council and the Mamdani administration, but also worker against boss. Operators of the more than 40 delivery service partners that zip across the city on trucks, bicycles and on foot say that the Council’s efforts would destroy their business, while some workers say the current model is exploitative and their jobs are already unstable. Amazon has rejected claims that its model makes these entities little more than — as the mayor and some top aides have called them — “shell companies” that shield the online behemoth from accountability. “These aren’t shell companies — they’re 4,500 entrepreneurs across 22 countries who’ve built real businesses, generated $75 billion in revenue, and created hundreds of thousands of jobs,” said Amazon spokesperson Steve Kelly, citing nationwide numbers. “The vast majority are running profitable, growing operations — and profitability has improved year over year,” he said. Small Business, Big Business Among them is Rudy Cazares, a former Marine Corps officer who said his company, Cazar Logistics, will go out of business if the City Council gets its way. “Delivering packages for Amazon has given opportunities for individuals like myself to be successful and provide an opportunity for individuals who wouldn’t have this opportunity if they applied to corporate America,” he said. Owners of delivery companies say they don’t recognize the way Mamdani and proponents of the bill have portrayed them. One owner left a job in finance to start a company that pays its drivers more than $27 an hour and offers a $5,000 tuition reimbursement. A driver for another company left FedEx because, he says, his Amazon delivery company pays better. Other workers say their companies offer chances for advancement that they can’t get in the corporate world because they lack college degrees. An Amazon delivery truck makes stops in Manhattan, May 6, 2026. Credit: Alex Krales/The City Reporter “I think that small businesses have a purpose and they certainly offer a benefit for me as a person with not a huge intellectual background but a breath of lived experience,” said Shannon Lindley, a high school graduate who is general manager at a Midtown logistics hub. “I can get somewhere in this small company.” While Amazon has threatened to shut down delivery operations in New York City should the bill pass, workers say the company already regularly yanks jobs away. In August, the Teamsters charged Amazon and 13 subcontractors with violating the state’s WARN Act by failing to give the approximately 1,300 workers at least 90 days’ notice of their impending terminations, according to a complaint filed to the state labor department. Earlier this month, Amazon severed its contract with a Delancey Street-based subcontractor that provided same-day delivery on electric cargo bikes. Two hundred workers were laid off overnight. Notice of the impending layoff does not appear on the state’s WARN notice dashboard, in another apparent violation of state law, Streetsblog reported . “They have these random ads, talking about ‘We care so much about Black and brown entrepreneurship’ — they just fired 200 black and brown workers in a company owned by a Black man,” one of the laid-off workers, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told The City Reporter. The worker says he supports the Delivery Protection Act because it would allow workers like himself to directly hold Amazon accountable. One expert compared Amazon’s forceful objection to the bill with Uber’s push to block a measure that raised drivers’ minimum pay rates. Just as Amazon warned of higher delivery costs, Uber said it would have to pass on fees to its passengers as well — and at one point threatened to shut down operations in New York. “Amazon gets away with making claims that are just totally false,” said Elizabeth Pancotti, vice president of policy, advocacy and research at the Groundwork Collective , a left-leaning think tank. “Uber made the same empty threats and look at that — it is easier than ever to get an Uber ride in New York City.” From the Trenches Jorge Arias, who until recently worked at a Maspeth-based delivery service partner, said he and his coworkers were pulled into a meeting on the dangers of the Delivery Protection Act. He still supports the bill. “They said if the Delivery Protection Act passes, we’re going to be like the UPS drivers: ‘They don’t have new vans, but you have new vans,’” recalled Arias. “And I’m thinking, you know, most Prime vans are broken.” Local delivery companies say they’re providing good, flexible jobs at good wages. A pop-up message from the Amazon app says a proposed city law regulating delivery workers could add a $5 charge to each purchase consumers make at the online retail giant, Nov. 23, 2026. Credit: Screenshot Logistics veteran Christine Chen set out two years ago to take advantage of Amazon’s enormous market share. While Amazon says it costs about $30,000 to establish a delivery company, Chen put in more than $60,000 to get Highgate Logistics off the ground — money well spent, she added. She uses bikes to deliver packages in Harlem. Staffing up for the holiday season, Chen now employs about 220 people earning $21 an hour, or $4 more than the city’s minimum wage. She offers health care, dental and vision insurance, plus a 401K match. Devon Smith, 23, a dancer with the Alvin Ailey Dance Theater, has been working for Chen since June. He works mornings so he can attend rehearsals in the afternoon, earning about $700 for 30 hours a week. “As artists, we work hard but it costs money to survive in the city,” he said. “Artists are terrible at jobs, but this is something we can do. It’s not the same thing every day and people interact with you — which is rare in New York City.” The Media War Council Speaker Julie Menin is reportedly moving to finally put the bill up to a vote on Dec. 3. The speaker, a former city consumer protection commissioner, has not taken kindly to Amazon’s tactics. Council Speaker Julie Menin (D-Manhattan) joins Mayor Zohran Mamdani a Bushwick community service organization to speak about speeding up the payment process for nonprofits that contract with the city, Oct. 8, 2026. Credit: Ben Fractenberg/The City Reporter “To put out an ad that falsely claims that if you purchase something on Amazon you’re gonna get socked with a $5 fee apiece, every single time, is completely misleading and deceptive, and it does not add to the negotiation we’re trying to have,” Menin said on Thursday in response to questions from The City Reporter. “I have made very clear from the start that we are not going to do something that will cause us to lose those jobs in New York City,” Menin said. The Five Borough Jobs Campaign, a longstanding business group, spent $2.3 million on anti-DPA ads between September and October. Amazon bankrolled that group to the tune of $5 million in the first six months of 2026, New York Focus reported . Meanwhile, Mayor Mamdani hasn’t been shy about using his physical and digital bully pulpit in support of the bill . On Monday, he said there was “a worker safety crisis” and that the DPA would “put in place some basic guardrails to regulate what is an expanding last-mile industry.” Is This Going to Become Law? The bill’s passage is still not guaranteed. In its current version, the bill has enough supporters in the Council to ensure its passage, and Mamdani has endorsed the measure as it stands today. But Menin is reportedly weighing changes before it is put for a vote, including a compromise that would still allow third parties to handle package deliveries so long as they are “true independent contractors,” City & State reported. The Fight Over Who Employs Amazon’s NYC Drivers appeared first on The City Reporter .

items.originalTitle: Fertility technology alone won't reverse global fertility decline, experts warn
items.title: Fertility technology alone won't reverse global fertility decline, experts warn
items.summary: Advances in fertility medicine have helped millions to have children—but a new international review published in Frontiers in Science has concluded that such treatments are unlikely to reverse the worldwide fall in fertility rates on their own.

items.title: Wall Street Set to Bounce Back After Tech Sell-Off
items.summary: Early stock market moves pointed to some stability when regular trading resumes in the United States on Monday, partly reversing a sharp fall last week. But analysts warned of more volatility ahead.

items.originalTitle: Local measurements reveal global quantum properties in a constant number of experimental runs
items.author: Zhenyu Du; Xiongfeng Ma
items.title: Local measurements reveal global quantum properties in a constant number of experimental runs
items.summary: A quantum device with more qubits is harder to verify. Describing a general quantum state takes an exponential number of parameters, and reconstructing it in full—a procedure known as state tomography—becomes impractical as the system grows. Yet most experiments do not need the full description. They need to know a few things: Is the state close to the target? Are the qubits entangled? And does the system carry the resources needed for quantum computation?
